lesson.title: den / einen / ihn Case Gym
lesson.subtitle: Eighteen accusative-object drills with the table words you own

hook.title: The Gym Is Open
hook.content: You know the secret: only the masculine raises its hand for direct objects — der → den, ein → einen, er → ihn — while feminine and neuter stand still. What you need now is repetition until the reflex is instant. The gym equipment is your own vocabulary: Kaffee, Tee, Tisch, Traum, Tag, Haus, Glas — plus three new props: der Stuhl, das Fenster, der Löffel. Reps, five machines, and every sentence is one you could furnish a room with.

footnotes.title: Why Drill This Case First
footnotes.content: The accusative is the case of DOING things to things — drinking, finding, bringing, seeking. It is the case you meet in every café sentence you will ever say. Master the masculine flag and 80% of everyday object sentences write themselves.

pattern.title: The Drill Circuit
pattern.content: Circuit one — articles: der Kaffee becomes den Kaffee when you drink it; der Traum becomes einen Traum when you have it. Circuit two — pronouns: ich sehe ihn (I see him), ich finde ihn (I find it). Circuit three — the untouched twins: die Zeit stays die Zeit, das Wasser stays das Wasser, no matter what you do to them. Circuit four — the full sentence: Ich trinke den Kaffee und esse den Apfel... every masculine object pays the -n toll; every feminine and neuter object rides free.
pattern.linguist_note: Notice der Tra(um) → einen Traum: the article carries the case flag, not the noun. German marks the object on the determiner — the same job English 'him' and 'whom' still do for pronouns.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase with its partner — masculine articles pay the -n toll as objects, and the last two are wir-forms for free:
exercises.target_answer: den Kaffee, einen Traum, den Tag, einen Tisch, den Stuhl, den Löffel, wir küssen, wir stehen
exercises.meaning: the coffee, a dream, the day, a table, the chair, the spoon (as objects), we kiss, we stand
exercises.explanation: Masculine objects pay the -n toll: der → den, ein → einen. The two wir-forms ride free — no object, no toll.

exercises.prompt: Complete: 'Wir halten _____ Löffel' (we hold the spoon):
exercises.explanation: Löffel is masculine and here it is the direct object: der → den.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence has NO accusative change — and why?
options: Ich habe dem Fenster — dative for windows
Ich habe den Fenster — the -n toll applies to all
Ich habe das Fenster — neuter objects stay unchanged
Ich habe des Fensters — genitive in rooms
exercises.target_answer: Ich habe das Fenster — neuter objects stay unchanged
exercises.meaning: Neuter and feminine ride free in the accusative
exercises.explanation: Only masculine singular marks the direct object. das Fenster, das Wasser, die Zeit — no flag change, ever.

exercises.meaning: Ich suche einen Kaffee = I am looking for a coffee
exercises.explanation: der Kaffee is masculine, sought and found: ein → einen.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'We put down the chair and show the spoon'
exercises.target_answer: Wir setzen den Stuhl und zeigen den Löffel
exercises.meaning: We put down the chair and show the spoon
exercises.explanation: Two masculine objects, two -n tolls — and one wir carries both verbs: setzen and zeigen keep their dictionary forms in the shared frame.

summary.outcome: Use den, einen, and ihn correctly with masculine direct objects across everyday sentences.
summary.takeaway: Masculine objects pay the -n toll (der → den, ein → einen); feminine and neuter stay unchanged.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Him & Whom — the proof texts where English still wears the ancient accusative on its sleeve.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from den / einen / ihn Case Gym (We put down the chair and show the spoon):
twist.target_answer: Wir setzen den Stuhl und zeigen den Löffel
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Wir setzen den Stuhl und zeigen den Löffel" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of den / einen / ihn Case Gym without relying on short-term echo.

die.etymology_derivation: th → d. Sounds identical to emphatic English "thee".

das.shift_rule: TH → D + T → S / SS / Z
das.etymology_derivation: Double shift: th → d and final t → s.

tisch.context_phrase: Der Teller steht auf dem Tisch.
tisch.context_translation: The plate stands on the table.
tisch.etymology_derivation: Latin discus → Old English disc (dish/desk) → Old High German tisc (tisch, with d → t).

tag.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and y → g.

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

stuhl.context_translation: The chair stands at the table.
stuhl.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *stōl — cognate with English stool; the meaning narrowed from stool to chair. [wiktionary]

fenster.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *fenestr, an early borrowing of Latin fenestra — a Latin loan both languages share. [wiktionary]

löffel.context_phrase: Nimm einen Löffel für die Suppe.
löffel.context_translation: Take a spoon for the soup.
löffel.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic lapilaz, from the root lap, meaning to lick or lap; English lap is the related word, and its p appears as f in German. [wiktionary]

stehen.context_phrase: Ich stehe am Fenster und sehe hinaus.
stehen.context_translation: I stand at the window and look out.
stehen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *stāną; the page documents cognate English stand, the same stand-verb family (English stood, German stand). [wiktionary]

zeigen.context_phrase: Kannst du mir den Weg zeigen?
zeigen.context_translation: Can you show me the way?
zeigen.etymology_derivation: From Old High German zeigōn, an intensive of zīhan; the page traces it to PIE *deyḱ- and notes that the root also gave Zeichen and English teach. The t of teach corresponds to the z of zeigen. [wiktionary]

küssen.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *kussijan — English kiss is the documented cognate; a doubled expressive kk that both languages kept. [wiktionary]

setzen.context_phrase: Ich setze mich auf den Stuhl.
setzen.context_translation: I sit down on the chair.
setzen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *sattjan, a causative of sit; the page documents cognate English set. The t of set reappears as z (ts) in setzen, the same sibilant shift as two and zwei. [wiktionary]

sitzen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + Ablaut Vowels
sitzen.context_translation: We are sitting in the café.

halten.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *haldaną — English hold is the documented cognate; German hardened d to t (the stop shift). Strong verb, class 7: hielt, gehalten. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
